note: Passage-centred pack, C1-C2, British English; a short talk on the post's synthesis: four layers of what a next-word predictor knows (text, structure, meaning, minds) and why the loss cannot tell you the kind of knowledge.

passage.text: A language model is trained to do one job: guess the next piece of text. It is scored by its loss, which measures how closely those guesses match real text. What it knows comes in four layers, from the most certain to the most contested. First come bits about text, which are measurable. That is knowledge in Claude Shannon's sense, and his theory sidesteps the question of meaning. Next is structure, such as grammar, which is well supported. Whether the model grasps meaning stands or falls on what you take meaning to be. As for minds, that is, tracking what people believe, the jury is still out. Models pass many tests, but small changes often break the result, which should give us pause. Yet people get some of those altered tests wrong too, so if a failure counts against the model, by the same token it counts against us. A low loss is not tantamount to understanding, and in and of itself it cannot tell you what kind of knowledge the model has. You can tease apart the kinds by changing the test in small ways and seeing what breaks.

gist.question: What four layers of knowledge does the speaker describe, and which is the most contested?
gist.answer: Bits about text, structure such as grammar, meaning, and minds. The question of minds is the most contested.

gist.question: What does a low loss not tell you, and how can you find out more?
gist.answer: It does not tell you what kind of knowledge the model has. One way to find out is to change the test in small ways and see what breaks.

retell.instruction: In 2-3 sentences, explain to a colleague why a low loss does not settle what an LLM knows.
retell.modelAnswer: A low loss, in and of itself, tells you how much a model knows about text, but not what kind of knowledge it is. One way to tease apart the kinds is to change the test in small ways and see what breaks. On whether models can track what people believe, the jury is still out.

items.definition: to succeed or fail completely depending on one particular thing
items.sentence: The validity of a surrogate-labelling study stands or falls on the quality of the human-coded sample it is checked against.

items.definition: people have not yet reached a decision or agreement about something
items.sentence: On whether these labels transfer to other platforms, the jury is still out.

items.definition: to make someone stop and think carefully, often with doubt
items.sentence: An agreement score that drops sharply on a second platform should give us pause.

items.definition: for the same reason; following the same logic
items.sentence: If we discount a classifier because it was tuned on its test set, then by the same token we should discount a hand-tuned dictionary.

items.definition: to be a reason for judging someone or something unfavourably
items.sentence: A single failed replication may count against a finding, but it rarely settles the matter.

items.definition: to be virtually the same as something else, in effect; the second thing is usually more serious or negative
items.sentence: Publishing only the runs that worked would be tantamount to hiding the ones that failed.

items.definition: considered alone, without other evidence or factors
items.sentence: A high agreement score is not, in and of itself, evidence that the codebook is valid.

items.definition: to separate two things that are closely mixed so that each can be examined
items.sentence: It is hard to tease apart the effect of the platform from the effect of the topic.

items.definition: to avoid dealing with a question or problem directly
items.sentence: The report sidesteps the question of causation by describing associations only.

items.headword: Inversion after a fronted ordinal (First come X, next comes Y)
items.definition: Put an ordinal or sequencing word first and the verb before its subject, so the list reads as a sequence: 'First come bits about text'. The verb agrees with the subject that follows, not with the fronted word.
items.sentence: First come the interviews; next comes the coding, and only then the analysis.
items.target: First come the interviews; next comes the coding

items.headword: Nominal clause 'what you take X to be'
items.definition: 'What you take X to be' asks for the speaker's view of X's nature and fits after 'depends on' or 'stands or falls on': 'Whether A is true stands or falls on what you take B to be'.
items.anchor: what you take meaning to be
items.sentence: Whether the corpus is representative depends on what you take the target population to be.
items.target: what you take the target population to be

items.headword: verb agrees with the subject after inversion
items.wrong: First comes bits about text, which are measurable.
items.definition: After a fronted 'First' or 'Next', the verb still agrees with the subject that follows: 'First come bits' (plural), but 'First comes grammar' (singular).

items.headword: no article with uncountable abstract noun
items.wrong: That is a knowledge in Claude Shannon's sense, and his theory sidesteps the question of meaning.
items.definition: 'Knowledge' is uncountable and takes no 'a' or plural in general use. 'A knowledge of X' is possible only with a modifier ('a working knowledge of X'). Say 'knowledge' or 'a piece of knowledge'.

items.headword: whether, not if, in a subject clause
items.wrong: If the model grasps meaning stands or falls on what you take meaning to be.
items.definition: A clause that is the subject of a sentence and expresses a yes/no question starts with 'whether', not 'if'.

items.wrong: Models pass many tests, but small changes often break the result, which should give us a pause.
items.definition: In the idiom 'give someone pause', 'pause' takes no article; 'a pause' means a short break in time or speech.

items.sentence: Loop the four core sentences until you can say them without the text; six of the pack's nine expressions will come with them, already in a natural rhythm.
